conflicts: Real-world figures are spreads from several sources and are kept side by side, never averaged; the maker interval is always given with them.
not_found: Brake pad life in hours: no public engine-builder, magazine or two-agreeing owner source with hour figures was found; makers say inspect every race and replace as required.
Wheel bearing and linkage/swingarm bearing replacement hours: makers publish inspection and greasing intervals only; no two agreeing public real-world hour figures were found.
Spark plug real-world life: makers publish intervals (e.g. Kawasaki 7.5 h, KTM two-strokes 15 h); no independent hour figures found.

Honda CRF450R/CRF250R 2020-on and Kawasaki KX450/KX250 2020-on: no two agreeing public reports with hours for how often the valves actually tighten on these generations (older-generation Honda titanium-valve reports exist but do not apply). Some owner-forum pages could not be read and were not used.

Riding type: amateur and pro motocross racing.

records.statement: Yamaha schedules a new piston, pin, clip and rings every fifth race (about 12.5 hours). In real use, testers and parts dealers put a 250F piston at about 25-40 hours for an amateur racer and a 450F at about 30-60 hours, with some 450 pistons run 100 hours as a gamble; a pro should change a 450 piston by about 20 hours. Owners racing at local level report 30-50 hours. Riding type: pro race vs amateur race; trail riders are not covered and often go longer. Measure ring gap, skirt and bore rather than assume.

records.statement: Yamaha schedules a valve-clearance check every third race (about 7.5 hours). Mechanics and owners widely agree that a valve clearance that keeps getting tighter means the valve face or seat is wearing (titanium intakes most often), that the time between adjustments then gets shorter, and that the lasting fix is new valves with the seats cut, usually new springs too, rather than repeated shims. Riding type: all; dirty air filters and running on the rev limiter speed it up.

values.maker_interval: a valve-clearance check every third race (about 7.5 hours)
values.sign: clearance moving tighter at each check; hard starting

source.name: Vital MX forum, Drastic valve adjustment (KX450)

records.notes: A valve maker also recommends a complete new valve and spring kit for engines at or past factory service limits.

records.topic: how often racers change the oil
records.statement: Yamaha schedules engine oil every third race (about 7.5 hours). Racers and owners commonly change engine oil much sooner, about every 3-5 hours or every race day, and some every ride on bikes where engine, gearbox and clutch share the oil; the oil filter is often done every second change. Riding type: amateur race and practice.

values.maker_interval: engine oil every third race (about 7.5 hours)

source.name: Vital MX forum, Oil change intervals...manufacturer recommendations

also_sources.name: Vital MX forum, 2023-24 Yamaha YZ450 engine hours/longevity

records.statement: Yamaha schedules fork oil every fifth race (about 12.5 hours). A suspension columnist services a hard-ridden practice bike every 10-15 hours, while a European suspension dealer quotes 20-40 hours depending on the bike; both say sand, hard riding and fast riders shorten it. Oil is usually the last thing to wear; bushings, seals, piston bands and shims go first. Signs: you keep going stiffer and slower on the clickers and they do less. Riding type: race and practice.

values.maker_interval: fork oil every fifth race (about 12.5 hours)

source.name: Motocross Action suspension column, when to service your fork and shock

records.topic: how often riders clean the air filter
records.statement: Yamaha schedules cleaning and oiling the air filter every race (about 2.5 hours). Most racers clean or swap the filter every ride day, many treat it as cheap insurance against valve and top-end wear, and some run 2-3 rides in clean conditions or use a filter skin; oil drying out or draining to the bottom of the foam is a reason to service it even when it looks clean. Riding type: race and practice; dust shortens it to every moto.

values.real_world: every ride day; 2-3 rides only in clean air
values.maker_interval: cleaning and oiling the air filter every race (about 2.5 hours)

records.statement: The maker gives no tire hour figure. Riding type: motocross race and practice vs trail.

records.topic: owner and tester valve reports, 2023-on YZ450F
records.statement: Yamaha schedules a valve-clearance check every third race (about 7.5 hours) and a new piston, pin, clip and rings every fifth race (about 12.5 hours). A long-term test found the 2024 YZ450F valve clearances still in spec at 17 hours, and owners of 2023-2024 YZ450Fs report 35-70 hours of local A, B and C racing with no valve or top-end problems and pistons that looked fine at 35 hours. Riding type: amateur race (sand and hard-pack).

records.topic: real-world two-stroke top-end life (testers, dealers, owners)
records.statement: Yamaha schedules a new piston every fifth race (about 12.5 hours) and new rings every third race (about 7.5 hours). Testers say a 125 piston and rings should be changed about every 15 hours for most riders and every 7 hours for a pro; a 250 two-stroke may go 40 hours for a local vet or novice but about 15 for a pro. A parts dealer gives about 25 hours in general, and owners report 125 rings at 10-15 hours and piston at 20-30, and 250 piston at 40-50. Riding type: pro race vs amateur race vs trail; lean jetting shortens it.
